title: Rapid recovery of vesicular dopamine levels in methamphetamine users in early abstinence

claims.statement: In people who had last used methamphetamine a mean of 2.6 days earlier, striatal binding of a vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) tracer was 28% higher than in controls (28 users, 22 controls), tracked recency and amount of use, and in the 17 who stayed abstinent did not differ from controls after a mean of about 10 days; the authors attribute the early rise to depleted vesicular dopamine competing less with the tracer, which the study could not test directly. Post-mortem VMAT2 in users was reported normal, and one PET study of long-abstinent users found binding about 10% lower.
claims.magnitude: Scan 1: whole striatum BPND 3.09 (SD 0.71) vs 2.41 (SD 0.34), +28%, p<0.0001 (editors' g about 1.24, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.85). Scan 2 (mean 9.9 days): 2.54 (0.39) in 17 abstainers vs 2.46 (0.34) in 9 controls, not different.

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established: lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found, but the measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation, some markers return toward normal with abstinence, and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in human users.
